import math
import random

class Value:
    """A number that remembers how it was made, so it can send gradients back."""
    def __init__(self, data, kids=(), op=""):
        self.data, self.grad = data, 0.0
        self._kids, self._op = kids, op
        self._backward = lambda: None
    def __add__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data + other.data, (self, other), "+")
        def _backward():
            self.grad += out.grad
            other.grad += out.grad
        out._backward = _backward
        return out
    def __mul__(self, other):
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data * other.data, (self, other), "*")
        def _backward():
            self.grad += other.data * out.grad
            other.grad += self.data * out.grad
        out._backward = _backward
        return out
    def __pow__(self, n):
        out = Value(self.data ** n, (self,), f"**{n}")
        def _backward():
            self.grad += n * self.data ** (n - 1) * out.grad
        out._backward = _backward
        return out
    def tanh(self):
        t = math.tanh(self.data)
        out = Value(t, (self,), "tanh")
        def _backward():
            self.grad += (1 - t * t) * out.grad
        out._backward = _backward
        return out
    def backward(self):
        order, seen = [], set()
        def visit(v):
            if id(v) not in seen:
                seen.add(id(v))
                for k in v._kids:
                    visit(k)
                order.append(v)
        visit(self)
        self.grad = 1.0
        for v in reversed(order):
            v._backward()
    __radd__ = __add__
    __rmul__ = __mul__
    def __neg__(self): return self * -1
    def __sub__(self, other): return self + (-other if isinstance(other, Value) else -other)
    def __repr__(self): return f"Value(data={self.data:.4g}, grad={self.grad:.4g})"

Because the policy needs to see every call to plan a route, and a call exists before any car is chosen

questions.q: Why make the scheduling policy its own object instead of writing the FIFO or SCAN logic inside the Elevator class?

With the policy as a separate object that has one method (choose), the elevator only asks it for a target, so you can swap FIFO for SCAN (or a new policy) without editing or re-testing the elevator, and compare them fairly on the same inputs. That's the strategy pattern; composition lets the Building plug in whichever policy it wants.

questions.q: In your own words: why does 2+3*4 give 14 in your calculator, even though nothing in the code says "do multiplication first"?
questions.a: Because the parser has one function per precedence level, and the + level gets its operands by calling the * level. So 3*4 is completely built (and becomes a subtree) before the + is combined. Evaluation is bottom-up, so deeper nodes are computed first. Precedence is the shape of the tree.

questions.q: Explain to a friend why a computer can differentiate any formula with just a handful of rules, and why it then has to simplify.
questions.a: Every formula is a tree, and each rule only needs to know the top node (a sum, a product, a sin) plus the derivatives of the children, which it gets by calling itself. Recursion walks the whole tree, so a few rules cover everything. But the rules are mechanical: they produce *1, +0 and repeated copies of subtrees. Without simplification those leftovers are carried and differentiated again, so the tree (and the time to evaluate it) grows explosively.

opts.t: It calls the loop body as a function
A JUMP instruction sets the program counter back to the loop's test
The stack remembers which line to repeat

questions.why: A loop is just a jump backwards; a JUMP_IF_FALSE at the test jumps forwards past the body when the condition becomes false. Every loop and if in every language you use comes down to these two jumps.

questions.q: Why does ADD need no operands, while PUSH and LOAD do?

opts.t: ADD always takes its inputs from the top of the stack, so there's nothing to name; PUSH and LOAD bring new values in from outside the stack
Operands are stored in a separate table

questions.why: That's the stack machine's big trade: instructions are tiny and the compiler never has to allocate registers, at the cost of more instructions shuffling values on and off the stack. Register machines (Lua 5, Dalvik) make the opposite trade.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a tree-walking interpreter and a bytecode VM, and how a while loop becomes bytecode.
questions.a: A tree-walking interpreter runs a program by recursively visiting its syntax tree every time code executes: evaluate the children, combine them. A compiler instead walks the tree once and emits a flat list of small instructions; a VM then runs that list with a program counter and a stack (fetch, advance, dispatch), which avoids re-walking the tree and is easy to optimise. A while loop compiles to: the condition's instructions, a JUMP_IF_FALSE to just after the loop, the body, and a JUMP back to the condition. The exit target isn't known when the JUMP_IF_FALSE is emitted, so it gets a placeholder that's patched after the body and the backwards jump are emitted.

questions.q: Why can a backtracking regex engine take 2ⁿ steps on a?a?…a?aa…a, while an NFA simulation with a set of states stays fast?
questions.a: Backtracking follows one path at a time; every ? is a choice, and when a later part fails it goes back and tries the other branch, so it can end up trying every combination of choices (2ⁿ). The NFA simulation never chooses: it keeps a set of all states the pattern could be in. A state is in the set at most once no matter how many paths reach it, so each text character costs at most (number of states) work: m × n in total.

questions.q: In a Bitcask-style store, what is on disk, what is in memory, and why can you lose the memory part safely?
questions.a: On disk: an append-only log of records (newest version wins, tombstones for deletes), split into segments that compaction rewrites to drop dead records. In memory: a hash index from each key to the byte offset (and length) of its newest record, so a read is one lookup plus one small disk read. The index is only a cache of where things are: after a crash you rebuild it by replaying the log from the start, and checksums let you detect and cut off a torn final write.

questions.why: Growing at the top is the whole secret of B-tree balance. Every path from root to leaf always has the same length, so the worst-case lookup is always the height: a few page reads, however unlucky the insert order.

questions.q: Explain why databases index tables with B-trees, how a B-tree stays balanced, and when an index doesn't help.
questions.a: Storage reads whole pages, so the goal is to touch as few pages as possible. A B-tree packs hundreds of sorted keys into each page-sized node, so the tree is only a few levels deep even for billions of rows; a lookup reads one node per level. Because keys are sorted, range queries and ORDER BY are an in-order walk, which a hash index can't do. It stays balanced because inserts go into leaves, and an overfull node splits and pushes its middle key up; only a root split adds a level, so every leaf is always at the same depth. An index doesn't help for conditions on columns it doesn't cover (that's a full scan), for queries that return most of the table, and it costs extra work on every insert.

questions.q: Why can git keep a full snapshot of your project in every commit without the repository exploding in size, and why does changing an old commit change every commit after it?
questions.a: Every object is named by the SHA-1 hash of its content. An unchanged file has the same hash, so a new tree just points at the existing blob: only changed files, their trees and the commit are new objects. A commit's text includes its parent's id, so its own id depends on the whole chain behind it; edit anything old and its id changes, which changes its child's text and id, and so on to the tip. That makes history deduplicated and tamper-evident.

questions.q: Why does a gap buffer make typing fast, why does vim need modes, and why does undo store commands instead of copies?
questions.a: A gap buffer keeps empty slots at the cursor, so typing just fills the next slot (O(1)); only moving the cursor shifts characters, one per step, and people type in bursts in one place. Modes let plain letters be commands in NORMAL mode and text in INSERT mode; a state machine (mode + key → action/next mode) keeps that straight. Undo stores each edit and how to reverse it (inserted X at p ↔ delete X at p), which costs as much memory as the edit itself, while a snapshot costs the whole document every time.

questions.q: Explain what happens inside a web framework between receiving a request and sending a response, and why middleware runs in the order it does.
questions.a: The server receives text over a socket. A parser turns it into a request: method, path, query, headers and body. The request passes through a stack of middleware: each is a function wrapping the next one, so it can act before (log, check auth, parse JSON) and after (record status, add headers, catch errors). The innermost layer is the router, which matches method and path against patterns, extracts parameters like an id, and calls one handler; no match gives a 404. The handler returns a response, which travels back out through the middleware in reverse, and is turned back into text with a status line, headers and body. The first middleware listed is the outermost, so it sees requests first and responses last, which is why logging goes on the outside and auth goes before the router.

questions.q: Walk through how a 3D triangle becomes coloured pixels, and say why the z-buffer beats sorting triangles.
questions.a: Rotate and move the triangle's corners with matrices, then divide x and y by depth to project them onto the screen (perspective). For every pixel, edge functions say whether its centre is inside; barycentric weights interpolate the depth there. A z-buffer stores the nearest depth seen so far at each pixel, and a triangle only paints a pixel when it's nearer. Sorting whole triangles needs one depth per triangle, which is impossible when triangles cross or overlap cyclically; the z-buffer decides each pixel separately, so order never matters.

questions.q: Explain how a CPU adds two numbers starting from transistors, why the carry makes it slow, and how the same circuit subtracts.
questions.a: Transistors make NAND gates, and NAND alone can build NOT, AND, OR and XOR. A full adder adds one column of bits plus a carry in: the sum is the XOR of all three, and the carry out is 1 when at least two are 1. Chaining full adders, each carry out feeding the next carry in, gives a ripple-carry adder for any width. It's slow because the top column has to wait for the carry to travel up from the bottom, two gate delays per bit; carry-lookahead logic computes the carries for groups of bits in parallel to fix this. In two's complement the top bit counts negative, so the same adder handles signed numbers, and negation is "flip the bits and add 1". To subtract, the CPU flips B's bits and sets the bottom carry in to 1, so one adder does both jobs. Around the ALU sit registers, memory and a program counter, and the CPU loops: fetch, decode, execute.

questions.q: Explain how an operating system shares one CPU and one memory between many programs, and the main trade-offs in each.
questions.a: The scheduler keeps a ready queue and gives the CPU to one process at a time. First-come-first-served is simple but short jobs get stuck behind long ones. Shortest-first minimises average waiting but needs to know the future and can starve long jobs. Round robin gives each process a time slice and sends it to the back of the queue, so interactive work stays responsive without knowing job lengths; smaller slices mean better response but more context switches, each of which costs time and cache warmth. For memory, each process uses virtual addresses split into a page number and an offset; a per-process page table maps pages to physical frames, which isolates programs from each other. A missing page causes a page fault; when memory is full the OS evicts a page, and LRU (evict the least recently used) works well because recent use predicts future use, while FIFO can even get worse with more memory. Because the scheduler can switch between any two instructions, shared data needs locks to avoid lost updates.

questions.q: Explain how a garbage collector decides what to free, and compare reference counting with mark and sweep.
questions.a: An object is alive if the program can reach it by following references from the roots: variables on the stack and globals. Reference counting stores a count of incoming references on each object and frees it the moment the count hits zero, cascading to its children; it's immediate and needs no pauses, but every assignment costs a little, and cycles leak because their counts never reach zero. Mark and sweep traces from the roots, marking everything reachable, then sweeps the heap and frees whatever wasn't marked; it handles cycles naturally but has to pause or run concurrently with the program. Real systems combine ideas: Python uses reference counting plus a cycle collector; Java and Go use tracing collectors, often generational because most objects die young, and sometimes copying to compact memory.

questions.q: Explain how lossless compression works, using Huffman coding and LZ77, and what limits it.
questions.a: Compression removes predictability. Huffman coding gives short codes to common symbols and long codes to rare ones: start with one tree per symbol weighted by its count, repeatedly merge the two lightest, and read each code as the left/right path from the root. Because symbols sit only at leaves, the codes are prefix-free, so the bit stream decodes without separators. LZ77 handles repetition: it replaces a repeated chunk with a back-reference saying how far back to look and how much to copy, and copies may overlap to produce runs. DEFLATE (ZIP, gzip, PNG) runs LZ77 then Huffman. Shannon's entropy, minus the sum of p log2 p, is the lower bound on average bits per symbol for a source, and the pigeonhole principle means no compressor can shrink every input: some must grow, which is why random or already-compressed data doesn't compress.

questions.q: Explain how a search engine finds and ranks documents quickly, and why rare words count for more.
questions.a: Ahead of time, every document is tokenized (lower-cased, split into words, often stemmed) and an inverted index is built: for each word, a sorted posting list of the documents containing it. questions.q: Explain how TCP delivers a reliable, in-order stream over a network that drops, corrupts and reorders packets.
questions.a: Every packet carries a sequence number and a checksum. The receiver discards damaged packets, buffers ones that arrive early, delivers data to the application only in order with no gaps, and sends cumulative acknowledgements naming the next sequence number it needs. Stop-and-wait is reliable but sends one packet per round trip, so TCP keeps a sliding window of many packets in flight. questions.q: Explain how Raft keeps five servers agreeing on one log while servers crash and come back.
questions.a: Time is split into terms, each with at most one leader. Followers that hear nothing from a leader for a random timeout become candidates, start a new term and ask for votes; a server votes once per term, and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date (later last term, or same last term and at least as long). A majority of votes makes a leader, and any higher term seen in a message makes a server step down. The leader appends client writes to its log and sends them in AppendEntries, which also carry the index and term of the preceding entry; a follower rejects a mismatch, and the leader backs up until the logs agree, then the follower's log is overwritten to match. An entry from the leader's current term stored on a majority is committed, and everything before it with it; committed entries are applied to the state machine in order on every server. Because any two majorities overlap and the vote rule refuses out-of-date candidates, every future leader already has every committed entry. With a majority down, nothing can be elected or committed: Raft stays unavailable rather than letting servers diverge.

questions.q: Explain how a GPT predicts the next word, and what attention does inside it.
questions.a: Text is split into tokens by byte-pair encoding, and each token becomes an embedding vector. The model's job is to output, for every position, a probability for every possible next token; generating text means sampling a token from those probabilities (sharpened or flattened by the temperature), appending it, and repeating. Its scores against every word are query · key divided by √d, a causal mask removes future words with −∞, a softmax turns the scores into weights, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. questions.q: Explain how a blockchain lets strangers share a ledger that nobody can quietly rewrite.
questions.a: Each block holds its data, the hash of the previous block and a nonce, and its own hash covers all three. Because a hash changes completely when any input changes, editing an old block changes its hash, which breaks the link stored in the next block, and so on to the end: tampering is visible. Proof of work makes repairing it expensive: a block only counts if its hash starts with a number of zeros, which takes about 16^d tries to find but one hash to check. Nodes keep the valid chain with the most work, and honest miners keep extending theirs, so a cheater with less than half the computing power falls further behind; the chance of rewriting a block k deep shrinks exponentially in k. questions.q: Explain how a ray tracer turns a scene into an image, including shadows and reflections.

For shadows it casts a second ray from the point (nudged off the surface to avoid self-hits) toward each light; a hit nearer than the light means shadow. For mirrors it casts a reflected ray r = d − 2(d·n)n, traces it recursively up to a depth limit, and blends its colour in. Rasterizers draw objects one at a time and must fake these effects; a ray tracer gets them by asking what each pixel sees, at the cost of many more rays.

Walking back from the bottom-right corner gives the diff: a diagonal step on equal lines keeps a line, a step left adds a new line, a step up removes an old one. The changes are grouped into hunks with a few lines of context. The table costs one step per pair of lines, so git uses Myers' algorithm, whose work grows with the number of differences instead.

It can't send every sensor's value down the optic nerve, so it sends differences. That's why two identical greys look different on different backgrounds and why flat bands show Mach bands at their edges. Neural networks that learn their own kernels end up with edge detectors too.

So compression is a bet on which data is likely, and Shannon's entropy gives the limit. Only what's predictable can be left out, so better compression needs better prediction, which is why noise can't be compressed and why a language model is a kind of compressor.

questions.a: A backend is a program listening on a port. A request arrives as text: a method (GET reads, POST creates, PATCH changes), a path, headers, and sometimes a body. The server matches the method and path together against its routes and runs exactly one handler; if nothing matches it answers 404. The status is the answer before the answer: clients read it first (res.ok means 200–299), so 201 means created, 400 means the client sent something wrong, 404 means no such thing, 409 means the move conflicts with the current state, and 5xx means the server broke. questions.q: Explain how a support bot's backend turns "where is my order?" into a real answer, and what keeps it safe and useful.
questions.a: Each message gets an intent: here by counting each intent's keywords and taking the most (ties to the first listed, no matches meaning it didn't understand); a language model can do the guessing instead, but every method is sometimes confidently wrong ("when will my refund arrive" counts as track). The bot keeps a session per customer, in Redis on a real server: the question it's waiting on and the last order number, so "it's 1042" answers "which order?" and "it" means 1042 later on; sessions expire after a quiet spell so yesterday's question can't be answered by accident. To answer with real data it calls tools: each has a name, a Zod schema for its arguments and code that runs it, which is exactly how language model tool calling works (the model writes the call, the server checks and runs it). A tool must check who's asking: an order that isn't the customer's gets the same reply as one that doesn't exist, and only the fields the answer needs leave the server; that check is in code, so no message, however persuasive, can talk its way past it. Replies are streamed as Server-Sent Events: text/event-stream, one "data:" line of JSON and a blank line per piece, then a done event and the end of the response. When the customer asks for a person or the bot misses twice in a row, it hands off: a ticket on the desk's queue with the whole transcript, and the bot goes quiet. Handing off at the first miss floods the desk (9 of 18 chats in the simulation against 4), and never handing off strands the customers it can't understand.
